strengths: The paper presents an interesting application of learned Levenshtein embeddings to short IDS-code construction and decoding. The stated exact radius-two exclusion procedure provides a sound minimum-distance-three codebook, independently of embedding accuracy.

Table 1 shows consistent improvements over random greedy selection across ten runs, reaching 16.8% greater maximum cardinality at length 11 and a normalized code rate of approximately 68.9%. These results provide useful initial evidence for the selection heuristic.

The decoder experiments include informative nearest-neighbor ablations: retrieving four neighbors produces no observed failures in 100,000 single-edit trials per tested length. Long-sequence experiments also investigate multiple-edit failures and demonstrate promising improvements with an outer Reed–Solomon code.

The flowcharts make the overall pipeline understandable, relevant prior embedding methods are acknowledged, and the manuscript explicitly identifies its redundancy conjecture as unproved. The synthetic-data experiments raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The central justification for codeword selection contains a mathematical error: batch normalization does not force embeddings to follow a multivariate Gaussian distribution (Section 3.2). Furthermore, low fitted Gaussian density is not shown to predict small Levenshtein neighborhoods. The observed improvements may remain valid, but the proposed mechanism needs direct empirical validation or a corrected argument.

The optimality claims substantially exceed the evidence. Matching a redundancy expression over short lengths up to 11 establishes neither finite-length optimality nor asymptotic order-optimality. No matching bound or certified optimum is supplied, and Figure 4 compares against asymptotic redundancy expressions without establishing their tightness at these short lengths. Acknowledging the conjecture is appropriate, but the abstract and introduction still overstate the conclusion.

The comparisons do not establish the value of the learned components sufficiently. Code construction is compared only with random selection, without minimum-neighborhood greedy heuristics, alternative density estimates, or ablations of the modified loss and learned embedding. Decoding is compared only with brute force, omitting natural exact baselines such as enumerating single-edit candidates and using codebook hash lookup. The headline 16.8% cardinality gain corresponds to approximately one percentage point of rate improvement over random selection at length 11.

Guaranteed correction by an exact bounded-distance decoder does not transfer automatically to the proposed embedding-based decoder. Exact reranking cannot recover a correct codeword excluded from the retrieved candidates. Zero observed failures in sampled trials supports empirical reliability, not the unconditional correction language used elsewhere; exhaustive single-edit validation or a guaranteed fallback is missing.

The complexity claims are inadequately supported. A kd-tree does not generally guarantee logarithmic nearest-neighbor query time, and the embedding dimension is unspecified. Figure 5 reports an increase from 6 to 367 seconds for k=1 as length increases from 7 to 11, providing little support for the claimed linear scaling. Construction over all 4^n candidates, index memory, and actual long-sequence DFS runtimes are not characterized.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The manuscript omits the precise base loss in Equation 5, embedding dimension, detailed network configuration, training-pair sampling, optimizer and training schedule, hardware, and DFS pruning thresholds. Section 3.6 promises a future code release rather than providing these essential details in the submission.

DNA-storage validation is confined to approximately 150-nucleotide sequences under one independent, balanced 1% IDS model. There are no matched end-to-end comparisons with cited practical systems or robustness studies for different error rates, error biases, and sequence constraints. The outer RS experiment also omits block lengths, arrangement across reads, and treatment of incorrect segment counts, making the claimed sufficiency of 2% parity difficult to reproduce or generalize.
